title: The Balance Sheet Equation
context: Analyze how the balance sheet equation requires total assets to equal the sum of total liabilities and total equity. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A pallet loader used by an operating business is classified as inventory because inventory can include any physical equipment a business owns.
A pallet loader held by a dealer for resale to customers is classified as a non-current asset because the dealer is a business rather than a household.
A pallet loader kept in service by an operating business for more than one year is classified as a non-current tangible asset.
The same pallet loader must always be classified identically on every balance sheet regardless of how it is held.
The same pallet loader may be a non-current asset for one business and inventory for another, depending on whether it is used or held for sale.
tactical_explanations:
Physical form alone does not make a pallet loader inventory. Inventory is held for sale or for cycle consumption — not every machine the firm owns.

Operating use beyond a year puts pallet loader among non-current tangibles. Counterexample: a forklift in the firm’s own warehouse is plant, not stock.

So the statement is False.

A dealer’s pallet loader held for customers is merchandise, not a non-current operating asset.

Being a business rather than a household does not turn trading stock into plant.

Counterexample: a pallet loader on the showroom floor stays inventory until sold.

So the statement is False.

Multi-year operating use of a pallet loader fits the non-current tangible test.

Useful life beyond the period plus own use — not resale — drive that line.

Tangible means physical substance; non-current means long-term benefit.

Ask whether the reporter uses the object or holds it for sale.

Benefit lasting beyond one year points non-current; trading-cycle stock points current. Physical durability never overrides that use-versus-resale split. The wording lines up with that rule, so the assertion stands.

So the statement is True.

The same pallet loader need not share one balance-sheet line everywhere. Each reporter classifies by how it holds the object.

Operator → non-current tangible; dealer → inventory. Physical identity does not freeze the category.

So the statement is False.

The same physical pallet loader need not share one balance-sheet line everywhere.

An operator using it beyond one year records a non-current tangible; a dealer holding it for customers records inventory.

Intended use — own operations versus resale — decides the line, which is exactly what the claim says.

So the statement is True.

context:

| Total assets | **1181** | **1279** |
| **EQUITY** | | |

Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Non-current assets normally have a useful life of more than one year and are intended to be used in the business for longer than one year.
Non-current liabilities amount to less than 56.8% of total equity in Year 2.
The combined total of equity and non-current liabilities exceeds non-current assets by more than 7.3% in Year 1.
Total equity grew by more than 24.5% between Year 1 and Year 2.
Total assets grew by more than 10% between Year 1 and Year 2.
tactical_explanations:
Non-current assets are held for use beyond one accounting period.

Useful life beyond a year plus operating intent define the category.

Ask whether the reporter uses the object or holds it for sale.

Benefit lasting beyond one year points non-current; trading-cycle stock points current. Physical durability never overrides that use-versus-resale split. The wording lines up with that rule, so the assertion stands.

So the statement is True.

Compute ncl-to-equity share as non-current liabilities ÷ total equity.

$$
\text{NCL share} = \frac{\text{non-current liabilities}}{\text{total equity}}
$$

Non-current liabilities combine the long-term loan and bonds lines:

From the extract: Equity = 839.

$$
\text{NCL} = 220 + 63 = 283
$$

$$
\frac{283}{839} \approx 0.3373 \approx 33.7\%
$$

The claim requires a result that less than 56.8%; the figures give Year 2 NCL/equity is 33.7%, which clears that test.

So the statement is True.

The working identity is Long-term financing surplus = (equity + non-current liabilities) ÷ non-current assets − 1.

$$
\text{Surplus} = \frac{\text{equity} + \text{NCL}}{\text{NCA}} - 1
$$

From the extract: NCA = 740.

$$
\text{Equity} + \text{NCL} = 761 + 267 = 1{,}028
$$

$$
\frac{1{,}028}{740} \approx 1.3892
$$

$$
\frac{1{,}028}{740} - 1 \approx 0.3892 \approx 38.9\%
$$

The surplus is 38.9%, which exceeds 7.3%.

So the statement is True.

Percentage growth for Total equity is (Year 2 − Year 1) ÷ Year 1.

$$
\text{growth} = \frac{Y_2 - Y_1}{Y_1}
$$

From the extract: Y_1 = 761, Y_2 = 839.

$$
Y_2 - Y_1 = 839 - 761 = 78
$$

$$
\frac{78}{761} \approx 0.1025 \approx 10.2\%
$$

The claim wants growth of more than 24.5%.

Compared with the claim (more than 24.5%), 10.2% is not enough for the wording to hold.

So the statement is False.

Percentage growth for Total assets is (Year 2 − Year 1) ÷ Year 1.

$$
\text{growth} = \frac{Y_2 - Y_1}{Y_1}
$$

From the extract: Y_1 = 1,181, Y_2 = 1,279.

$$
Y_2 - Y_1 = 1{,}279 - 1{,}181 = 98
$$

$$
\frac{98}{1{,}181} \approx 0.0830 \approx 8.3\%
$$

The claim wants growth of more than 10%.

Compared with the claim (more than 10%), 8.3% is not enough for the wording to hold.

So the statement is False.
